episode_title: Five Epic Stories That Must Be Films

stories.topic: The Sinking of the French Navy at Mers-el-Kebir
stories.summary: In the summer of 1940, after France capitulated to Germany, Churchill faced the prospect of the considerable French Navy falling into German hands and ending Britain's naval dominance. The Royal Navy went to Mers-el-Kebir in Algeria and pleaded with the French commanders to defect with their ships and join the Allies. The French refused — partly because of obedience to Marshal Petain's Vichy government, partly because of a delusion that France was still a 'first-class power' and a 'Vishwaguru.' Churchill gave the order, the Royal Navy opened fire, and 1,300 French sailors died.
stories.insight: Some decisions cannot be cleanly judged in hindsight — there is no clean line between 'right' and 'wrong' when civilisation itself is on the line. The cost of the right strategic move is sometimes measured in the lives of people who weren't actually your enemy, and an honest leader has to live with that ambiguity.

stories.topic: Silence of the Heart — ERP and the Couple Who Heard the World Differently
stories.summary: In 1926 AT&T set up Electrical Research Products Inc. (ERP) — a department of evangelists for clean theatrical sound that grew from 1,000 to 4,000 screens in the year 1929 alone, traveling the world with cap-whistles and knapsacks, treating silence as 'the devil' and reverberation as 'the sidekick of the devil.' Amit's pitch lays a fictional couple over this real history: both join ERP as fellow zealots, but slowly the woman starts hearing things differently from her husband and the rest of the team. At first she gaslights herself; later she owns it: 'Why is he right? Why am I wrong? This is how I listen. This is how he listens.'
stories.insight: We've seen many films of two people drifting apart because they see the world differently — almost none of two people drifting apart because they hear it differently. Differences in perception are usually invisible to us, and invisible drift is the hardest kind to repair.

stories.summary: Take a dataset of people who lost their eyesight after age five, after they had already learned to see. With careful training, two-thirds of them become able to orient themselves through echolocation — whistling and listening for the echo, exactly the way bats do. Some get so good at it that they can ride a bicycle outdoors, navigating traffic by sound. Amit pairs this with Krish Ashok's friend who listens to podcasts at 6x speed; Amit can manage 3.5x.
stories.insight: The brain has astonishing latent plasticity — capacities we don't know we have until a faculty is taken away. Thomas Nagel argued we can never know what it is like to be a bat; this data suggests, awkwardly, that some of us already know.

stories.topic: The Doolittle Raid — Hacking the B-25
stories.summary: After Pearl Harbor, striking Japan back was considered infeasible with conventional equipment. A team of engineers hacked the B-25 bomber in dozens of ways — adding fuel tanks, removing weight, adding de-icing — to give it ~80-90% more range. A carrier group sailed close to Japan; the bombers took off (planes that could take off from a carrier but not land back), bombed Tokyo, and were supposed to land on Kuomintang airfields in China (Stalin had refused Vladivostok). The carrier was spotted earlier than planned and the planes launched too far out, so most crashed in China; the Japanese then massacred ~70,000 Chinese soldiers and ~250,000 civilians as reprisal. One plane reached Vladivostok — its crew was 'fake-escaped' by the NKVD into Iran. Coming just four months after Pearl Harbor, it shattered Japanese complacency.
stories.insight: Excellence comes from hacking, not just using. There is one tier of the world where you buy equipment and use it as instructed; another, much smaller tier where you understand it well enough to take it apart and adapt it to do something nobody had imagined. The same lesson generalises far beyond bombers.

stories.summary: When the Japanese ship spotted the American carrier group it desperately radioed Tokyo before being destroyed. But Japan's response was to mobilise for a naval engagement — they could not imagine that planes might take off from the carrier, hit Japan, and continue on to China. The B-25s had been hacked, but no one on the Japanese side had imagined that hack.
stories.insight: The most expensive form of blindness in war (and in business) is imaginative — you cannot defend against an attack you cannot conceive of. 'Fighting the last war' is the canonical version of this failure.

stories.topic: The Boy Who Burned His School — V.P. Menon's Origin
stories.summary: A Malayali schoolboy is failed in his exam for poor attendance and sent home. He sits at the railway station with his cold lunchbox, walks by the river, sleeps under a tree, wakes at dusk and finds an empty liquor bottle, walks to a liquor store, buys a bottle 'on his mother's account,' asks for a matchbox — and sets the school on fire. He runs away on a train to Kolar, works the goldmine fields, then drifts to Bombay as a towel salesman. In Delhi station his pocket is picked; a passing Sardarji hears his story and gives him ten rupees — a fortune in 1916. He never gets the man's name. The boy joins the government, considers leaving after the Rowlatt Act, decides 'sometimes some people have to stay within to change the world,' and becomes V.P. Menon — the bureaucrat who, with Sardar Patel, integrated 500+ princely states into India.
stories.insight: History pivots on the smallest acts. Without ten rupees from an anonymous Sardarji, India might literally have been a different country. Great historical figures are not born great; they are dragged into it by anger, accident, and the kindness of strangers.

stories.summary: When the Nawab of Junagadh realised he could not actually take his kingdom to Pakistan, he chartered a plane to flee with everything he loved. The treasury was loaded in. The dogs were loaded in. The begums and children were loaded in. As the plane was about to take off, one begum cried out: 'Wait, my child is still in the palace!' The Nawab looked around, counted the dogs, found them all present — and told that begum, 'I love you, it was nice knowing you. Please get off.' The plane took off for Karachi.
stories.insight: A blackly comic compression of the entire princely-states project — 547 kingdoms, 547 absurd stories. Folded inside any 'grand' history are vignettes of casual cruelty that no statute or treaty can capture.

stories.summary: Mountbatten and V.P. Menon are negotiating with Hanwant Singh, the portly young Maharaja of Jodhpur, who is being tempted by Jinnah's offer of a 'blank cheque' to join Pakistan. They eventually persuade him; he is about to sign. Mountbatten leaves. Menon is alone with him. Hanwant Singh's pen turns out also to be a gun. He raises it at Menon. Menon, in Amit's cinematic imagining, simply raises an eyebrow and smiles. Hanwant Singh signs. Years later, in the early-to-mid 1950s, the same Hanwant Singh telephones Menon and offers to make him MP from Jodhpur.
stories.insight: Negotiation under duress is a class of skill we underrate — the ability to stay still when a gun is pointed at you, and to convert that stillness into an outcome. India was assembled by men who could do that.

stories.summary: Russia, the world's second-most powerful army, smashed into Ukraine in February 2022 expecting an Afghanistan-style collapse. Zelensky — a former TV comedian who once played a piano with his penis on a comedy show, and who had played a fictional Ukrainian president in a sitcom — was offered evacuation. He stayed. NATO intelligence had penetrated the Russian side from the inside out (heroic Russian patriots leaking everything); Ukraine had partially prepared, moving key defence assets just before the first Russian strikes hit empty sites. Russia briefly captured Hostomel airport in a paratrooper op; in the chaos that followed, Ukraine caught its breath and mounted what Ajay calls the greatest underdog scrappy defence in modern history. Zelensky was simultaneously fighting Western disdain — Macron, German appeasement, Obama-era acquiescence to Crimea 2014.
stories.insight: The world's pessimists were wrong on every dimension at once: Russia wasn't as strong as it looked, Ukraine wasn't as weak as it looked, the comedian was a leader, and Western disdain was a far bigger obstacle than Russian arms. 'I don't want a ride; I want ammunition' is the line, but the lesson is that scrappy improvisation beats expensive incompetence.

stories.topic: Hostomel and the History of Paratrooper Attacks
stories.summary: Paratroopers go behind the lines, capture critical assets — typically an airfield — and create a bridgehead so that heavy equipment can be air-delivered and the main force can link up. The model case is Hitler's 6,000-paratrooper capture of Crete in 1941. The cautionary case is Arnhem ('A Bridge Too Far'), where the paratroopers seized the bridges but the main force never reached them, and they were killed or captured. At Hostomel airport in 2022, the Russians actually captured the airfield — but the chaos that followed gave Ukraine its opening rather than Russia its bridgehead.
stories.insight: Paratrooper operations are pure timing — they only work if the relief column arrives. The same logic applies far beyond the military: any bold first move that requires a second mover to succeed. Be very careful before you parachute in.

recommendations.creator: David Byrne
recommendations.context: Byrne is the frontman of Talking Heads; the book is, Amit says, the best book he has ever read about music.
recommendations.reason: It's incredibly meta — it goes into the whys and into Amit's own obsession with how form shapes the world. Byrne's imagined description of the ERP men listening like 'acoustic Sherlock Holmes' is the seed for the second story Amit pitches in this episode.

recommendations.creator: William Spaniel
recommendations.context: A YouTube channel by a political scientist (also a published author) that has run the best running explainer of the Battle of Kiev as it unfolded.
recommendations.reason: He combines first-draft-of-history (videos in real time) with slower considered books — exactly the dual register Ajay argues this age demands.

recommendations.creator: Emily Thompson
recommendations.context: A historical essay on ERP — Electrical Research Products Inc. — and the global evangelism of clean theatrical sound in the 1920s and 1930s.
recommendations.reason: The factual backdrop of Amit's 'Silence of the Heart' film pitch — Thompson tracks how ERP grew, how the French burned a theatre down to repel the evangelists, and how the Indian film industry eventually told them to get lost.

recommendations.item: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
recommendations.creator: Thomas Nagel
recommendations.context: Nagel's 1974 essay on the irreducibility of subjective experience — we can describe echolocation but cannot inhabit a bat's experience of it.
recommendations.reason: Amit invokes it as the 'data point against' Ajay's claim that humans can be trained to echolocate — until he realises the second data point (Krish Ashok's blind friend listening at 6x) is in support of Ajay.

recommendations.item: A Scientist in the Kitchen — Episode 204 of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok
recommendations.context: Amit's first long episode with the writer Krish Ashok, in which Krish discussed how he listens to podcasts at high speeds.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 6x-listening anecdote about Krish's blind friend — the second data point in Amit's exchange with Ajay about brain plasticity.

recommendations.item: India's Greatest Civil Servant — Episode 167 of The Seen and the Unseen

recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Narayani Basu, V.P. Menon's granddaughter, on his life.
recommendations.reason: The fuller version of the V.P. Menon story that Amit pitches as one of the five must-be-films — the boy who burned down his school and grew into the executor of India's integration.

recommendations.item: VP Menon: The Unsung Architect of Modern India
recommendations.creator: Narayani Basu
recommendations.context: Basu's biography of her grandfather V.P. Menon, source of the boyhood-arson story and the train journey to Kolar.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a 'marvellous book' and credits it explicitly for all the details of Menon's early life that drive his pitch.

recommendations.creator: V.P. Menon
recommendations.context: Menon's own account of the integration of the princely states.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show's resources alongside Basu's biography as a primary source for the nation-building story.

recommendations.creator: Volodymyr Zelensky
recommendations.context: Pre-political comedy clip of Zelensky playing a piano with his penis.

recommendations.context: Ryan's classic account of Operation Market Garden — the failed Allied paratrooper landings at Arnhem.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes it as the cautionary case in his potted history of paratrooper warfare: a brilliant invasion plan that failed because the main force never reached the bridgehead.

recommendations.creator: Talking Heads
recommendations.context: Amit's first encounter with Talking Heads — switching on music television in mid-1990s post-liberalisation India and being completely blown away.
recommendations.reason: A personal hinge point: post-1991 India opened, MTV arrived, and a single song could rearrange a young Indian's musical universe. The artefact of the Reformers' work, made tangible.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The earlier episode of EIE in this same 'stories that should be films' genre.
recommendations.reason: Referenced as the predecessor — this episode is the second instalment in that genre, with five more pitches.

recommendations.item: The Reformers — Episode 28 of Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous week's episode on India's economic reformers.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'a great story on its own' and explicitly thanks 'the group of people we spoke about in the last episode' — the Reformers — for opening up India in the 1990s and bringing music television to him.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's recurring frame, applied here to the integration of India: the moment you say 'the end justifies the means,' you can construct any end in your head and commit any brutality. So even when you love the resulting India, you can hold a 'deep disquiet' about how it was assembled — through coercion and broken promises by Patel and Menon. He calls it 'fast-track colonisation' — what the British did over 200-300 years, India did to itself in two.
core_ideas.quote: It is very important to me that we always consider the means as something supremely important.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's meta-lesson from the Doolittle Raid: the world has two tiers. One is the tier of users — people who buy other people's creations and use them in normal ways. The other is the tier of hackers — people who understand the equipment well enough to take it apart, modify it, and do something nobody had ever imagined. Excellence and amazing things happen at the second tier. The B-25 bomber was modified in dozens of ways to make a strategically infeasible mission feasible.
core_ideas.quote: You can be a dumb user of other people's creations, or you can know enough about them that you are able to take it apart and modify it and adapt it and do something new that had never before been imagined.

core_ideas.explanation: Despite having been humiliated by Germany, having been saved by the British and Americans in 1914, having lost to Napoleon's British, and having watched the French Navy destroyed by the British at Trafalgar, France in 1940 still nursed a self-conception as a first-class power and a Vishwaguru — a unique civilisation with novel philosophy to give the world. That delusion is what made it humiliating to defect to the British side, and so the French Navy at Mers-el-Kebir refused — and 1,300 sailors died for it. Ajay extends the term knowingly — every country has its Vishwaguru moment.
core_ideas.quote: Some of these delusions in France of being a first-class power, of being an equal to the UK and America, of being a Vishwaguru.

core_ideas.explanation: Films and novels routinely show people drifting apart because they see the world differently. Amit's pitch turns on a less examined truth: people also hear the world differently. Two people in the same room — Amit, Ajay, and the cinematographers — would describe the soundscape in different ways without being able to articulate the difference. In a relationship, that invisible drift can do as much damage as a visible disagreement, and a film could literalise it with separate sound filters per character (a possibility in Dolby Audio).
core_ideas.quote: We have seen so much cinema in which two people drift apart because they see the world differently. But imagine two people drifting apart because they hear the world differently.

core_ideas.concept: Brain Plasticity Is Bigger Than We Think
core_ideas.explanation: Two-thirds of people who lose sight after age five can be trained to echolocate well enough to ride a bicycle in traffic. Krish Ashok's blind friend listens to audio at 6x. The brain reallocates faculty when one is taken away — this is not exotic; it is statistical. The implication: each of us is sitting on cognitive capacities we don't know we have. We just haven't been forced to discover them.
core_ideas.quote: This is the power that resides inside each of us. We are just not aware of it.

core_ideas.concept: Stakes Drive Drama (Academic Politics Is So Vicious Because the Stakes Are So Low)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's argument for why the Second World War keeps producing great films: the fate of the world was on the line, life-and-death decisions for individuals were also fateful for civilisation. The Falklands War is a counter — high heroism but low stakes — and so no one wants the movie. He inverts this with the famous quip about academic politics: the politics is vicious precisely because the stakes are negligible.
core_ideas.quote: Why is academic politics so vicious? The answer is because the stakes are so low.

core_ideas.explanation: The Japanese ship saw the American carrier group and signalled Tokyo before being destroyed. But Tokyo could not imagine planes flying off the carrier, hitting Japan, and continuing on to China — that was not in their model of the possible. So they prepared for a naval engagement and got a bombing raid. The most expensive form of blindness in war is imaginative — and 'fighting the last war' is its standard form.
core_ideas.quote: That imagination of the raid was not available to the Japanese side.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay and Amit play with two counterfactuals. What if India hadn't taken Goa — would Goa now be in the European Union, with first-world institutions, a Hong Kong on the subcontinent? What if the British had kept Surat as their charter city? What if the Sardarji had not given Menon ten rupees, and India had instead remained 30 or 50 or 500 entities — not 'balkanisation' but a competitive federation of small jurisdictions, each forced to govern well? Ajay's counter-counter: most princely states had appallingly underdeveloped political institutions and would have made bad democracies. Counterfactuals are how you stress-test the claim that current arrangements are the only possible ones.
core_ideas.quote: It need not have been this way. It could have been a million different things.

core_ideas.explanation: The standard story of the Battle of Kiev is Zelensky vs Putin. Ajay reframes it: Zelensky was simultaneously fighting Russian arms and Western disdain. Macron, German appeasement, Obama's acquiescence to the 2014 Crimea grab — for many in Western Europe, this was just another Crimea, just give Putin some land and move on, the calendar is full. Pessimists assumed a comedian could not lead, that Ukraine would collapse like Afghanistan. The first weeks of Kiev's defence were almost entirely Ukrainian — the West showed up afterwards, partially.
core_ideas.quote: There was a genuine part of Western Europe which was in no mood to deal with this.

core_ideas.explanation: Journalists write the first draft of history; later, more considered accounts emerge. Ajay's recommendation of William Spaniel illustrates the strange new feature of this age — the same person can do both at once, posting real-time YouTube analysis and writing slow, careful books. Amit observes that we now consume both registers simultaneously, which used to be impossible.
core_ideas.quote: You have both the first draft of history and the sense-making happening simultaneously.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's frame for his ERP pitch: a story works when its grand-scale frame contains a small-scale relationship that mirrors it. ERP's ideological zeal — 'one way of looking at the world' coming to a fall — contains the relationship of one couple, where the woman's quiet refusal to keep agreeing with her husband's hearing is a refusal of the same kind of monoculture. The macrocosm and microcosm rhyme.
core_ideas.quote: A macrocosm of ideological zeal and one way of looking at the world coming to a fall can also contain the microcosm of the relationship of these people.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on his kurta misbehaving on camera: 'My mic flipped out from inside and came outside.' Ajay's deadpan diagnosis — 'the structural integrity of his kurta is suspect' — is met with: 'That is such a military analyst phrase. Structural integrity of the kurta.' Amit then realises he wore the same kurta for the previous storytelling episode and submits to being christened 'Kurta Cobain.'
Ajay on Amit's stylistic tic: 'No ships are being scuttled. Ships are destroyed. The zeal with which you use the word destroyed.'
Amit: 'Even though your commander is a guy called Doolittle. Like Naam de hi haika. Kaisi motivate karoge.' On the awkwardness of motivating troops led by an officer literally named 'Do little.'
Amit on Ajay's throwaway line: 'I love the way you say the stakes are so low like academic politics. You just like threw that in there, thinking no one will notice. But I'm gonna highlight it.'

Amit on Zelensky's pre-political CV: 'He had also done a comic act where he plays a piano with his dick. We will also link it from the show notes, but there will be no insert on the side. This is a family-friendly show.'
Amit on India and stand-up: 'India did not make Kapil Sharma the [president] — yet.' (Said in deflected horror at the parallel with Zelensky's path from comedy to presidency.)

Ajay on the cost-benefit of catastrophe to art and politics: 'It might have been a fatal sin of someone there that he was naval gazing and not navel-gazing.' On the Japanese commanders mistaking which kind of gaze was needed.
Amit on his typo: in his notes the V.P. Menon scene says 'sitting under a three.' He clarifies on air that it is meant to be 'tree.'

Ajay's ERP newsletter setup — 'they had a newsletter called — you have to guess the name. What was the name of the newsletter by Earpy? Aha. It's a slow day for you.' (The implied pun being a deliberate flat joke that lands by missing.)
Amit on the merchandise division of Amitbhai Media Private Limited: 'The request is instantly denied.' Ajay had asked for a second T-shirt: 'I don't want a ride, I want ammunition.'
Amit on the canine pun: 'If you got a dog and it was a spaniel, what would it be called? I'm just wondering. I don't have a punchline for this. Do tell us, gentle reader, in the comments.'
Patel asks Nehru, in 1940, about Hitler: 'Jawahar, ek baat batao yaar, kab harega woh haramzaada?' ('Jawahar, tell me, when will that bastard lose?') An anecdote on the founders' candour.
Zelensky's iconic refusal of US evacuation: 'I don't want a ride, I want ammo.'
'A Bridge Too Far' — Cornelius Ryan's title for the failed Allied paratrooper landings at Arnhem, invoked as the cautionary case study of paratrooper operations whose relief column never arrives.

David Byrne in How Music Works on the ERP men: 'Like some acoustic Sherlock Holmes. They could survey a room with their ears and be able to tell you things about it, even what was going on outside of it.' Quoted in full by Amit.

The Doolittle Raid plane that landed at Vladivostok, was interned by the Soviets, and was 'fake-escaped' by the NKVD into Iran — a piece of Cold-War-prefiguring choreography between technically-not-yet-allies.

Trump's 'perfect phone call' with Zelensky — Trump's attempted blockade of the Javelin missiles in exchange for a fake investigation against the Bidens. Ajay invokes it as the moment when Western support to Ukraine was nearly killed at birth.
'Once in a Lifetime' by Talking Heads — the song Amit first heard on Indian music television in the mid-1990s after liberalisation, his entry point into David Byrne's work.
